title: Two wills (8.9–8.10)
hookLine: he wants to change and doesn't want to, at the same time
tomorrow: what did young Augustine ask God for, with a catch?

cards: An alarm goes off at six. The same hand that could turn it off and get up hits snooze. Augustine noticed the strangeness of that in a garden in Milan.
He wills his hand to move, and it moves, so fast you can hardly tell the order from the doing. He wills his own mind to want God, fully, and it won't. The body obeys at once.

teach.h: THE BODY OBEYS. THE MIND RESISTS.
teach.b: The question is old: can one person want two things at once? Augustine's Latin puts it sharply: imperat animus corpori, et paretur statim; imperat animus sibi, et resistitur.
The mind commands the body and is obeyed at once; the mind commands itself and is resisted.
His answer: the mind doesn't will with the whole of itself. If it did, it wouldn't need to give the order. So there are two wills, an old one held by habit and a new one only beginning.
And here's his firm line: it was I who willed, and I who was unwilling. Not two strangers fighting inside him. One person, divided, and so one person who can be healed.
A neighbor tradition sits close to this.

The Jewish Mishnah reads the verse, in the JPS translation, "thou shalt love the LORD thy God with all thy heart", and says: with all your heart means with both your inclinations, the good inclination and the evil one, the yetzer.

teach.h: HEALED INTO ONE, OR BOTH FOR GOD?
teach.b: The Mishnah and Augustine both see one person pulled two ways, and both bring the whole divided heart to God.
One honest difference: Augustine calls the split a sickness that grace heals into one will. The Mishnah asks a person to love God with both inclinations, even the one that pulls the other way.

how: Catholics bring this kind of divided heart to prayer and to the sacrament of confession, and some turn to Augustine's account in Confessions 8 for words.

o: a contract signed by two people at once
wanting and not wanting at once, in one person
two rival spirits fighting over one person's soul

games.q: one person, divided — tap the pairs.

s: Augustine blamed an evil nature inside him that wasn't really him
it was I who willed, and I who was unwilling, he says. One person, divided.
the Mishnah reads 'with all thy heart' as both inclinations, good and evil
the good inclination and the evil one, the yetzer.
for Augustine, the mind obeys itself as easily as the body obeys it
the body obeys at once; the mind commands itself and is resisted.

games.q: a friend says, "my bad side isn't really me." which reply fits the Mishnah's reading of 'with all thy heart'?
o: love God with both inclinations, even the one that pulls.
cut the bad side off; only the good half counts.
the heart means only your good inclination.
games.why: the Mishnah reads 'with all thy heart' as with both inclinations. Augustine, from his side, insists both wills are his: 'it was I.'

practice: Pick one thing you both want and don't want to change. Give each will one plain sentence in your head, the one that wants it and the one that doesn't, then add a third: one small next step both could live with.
If you pray, you can hold all three before God, as one person.

wordCard.voice: Two wills. Augustine's name for wanting and not wanting at once: one person, divided, not two strangers.

orig.note: Latin for will; Augustine writes of an old will and a new one (Confessions 8.5).

carryVoice: Two wills, one person: the split is yours, and so both halves can be brought to God. Go in peace.
